title: Third-Party Data Isolation and Evidence Delivery Playbook (template)
summary: Negotiable template and operational playbook for contractual obligations around customer data segregation, evidence request SLAs, and audit/evidence delivery from vendors and subprocessors. Intended for inclusion as an exhibit or annex to DPAs and managed-service agreements.
content:
Purpose and intent:
This document is a contract-friendly playbook to be attached as an exhibit to a Master Services Agreement (MSA) or Data Processing Agreement (DPA). It defines minimum expectations for: (1) logical and administrative segregation of customer data; (2) timeliness and format of evidence provided to customers or auditors; (3) acceptance criteria for forensic artifacts and chain-of-custody; and (4) controls expected from subprocessors and hosting environments (including on-prem/hybrid deployments).

Scope:
Applies to: (a) vendor-managed hosted services, (b) dedicated/reserved capacity offerings, and (c) private/on-prem deployments where vendor provides maintenance, support, or remote access. Does not change substantive data-privacy commitments in the parent DPA; this playbook operationalizes the evidence and segregation obligations.

Definitions (short):
- "Customer Data": data the customer sends to the service or that is derived from customer inputs.
- "Isolated Environment": tenancy construct (project/tenant/VM/GPU-pool) configured to prevent cross-customer access.
- "Evidence Request": formal request from customer or authorized auditor for logs, snapshots, or forensic artifacts.
- "Proof-of-Deletion": verifiable artifact demonstrating data wipe in accordance with retention obligations.
- "Chain-of-Custody": dated record showing control and handling of forensic artifacts from collection to delivery.

Minimum data segregation requirements (negotiable):
1) Logical segregation: Customer workloads must run in an Isolated Environment by default. For multi-tenant infrastructure, the vendor must document and provide: configuration of namespaces/projects, RBAC boundaries, and per-tenant encryption contexts where supported.
2) Administrative controls: Separate admin accounts (no shared root for multiple customers), per-customer support keys/roles, and MFA for any privileged access.
3) Network segmentation: Dedicated VPCs, VLANs, or at minimum strict NSG/firewall rules preventing cross-customer traffic unless explicitly authorized.
4) KV-cache and prefix cache handling: KV caches and any in-memory token caches must be scoped per-customer. If cache reuse is performed to improve efficiency, vendor must disclose conditions and provide an opt-out for customers with higher isolation needs.

Evidence and artifact delivery SLA (template clauses):
- Acknowledgement: Vendor will acknowledge an Evidence Request within 24 hours of receipt.
- Initial response: Within 3 business days provide a containment assessment and list of available artifacts.
- Artifact delivery: Unless otherwise agreed, vendor will deliver preserved forensic artifacts (logs, config snapshots, storage snapshots, relevant telemetry) within 10 business days.
- Proof-of-Deletion: For deletion requests tied to retention or termination, vendor will provide a Proof-of-Deletion artifact within 15 business days (or shorter if required by law).
- Severity escalation: For incidents involving confirmed data exposure, vendor will prioritize artifact preservation and work with customer on a mutually agreed compressed timeline (typical target: initial artifacts <48 hours).
Note: timelines are negotiable for on-prem or air-gapped deployments where physical processes may add delay.

Artifact formats and acceptance criteria:
- Logs: Provide raw and parsed logs where possible (timestamps must be UTC, ISO-8601). Include log generation source, log retention IDs, and any parsers used.
- Snapshots: Storage volume or object snapshots should be tagged with snapshot-id, UTC timestamp, and the environment name.
- Process dumps/ram images: Only provided if specifically requested and subject to NDA and transfer controls; must be accompanied by a collection checklist.
- Cryptographic evidence: If encryption-at-rest keys were used, vendor should provide key identifiers, Keystore metadata, and redacted key wrapping logs sufficient for verification (never raw key material).
- Hashes and checksums: Provide SHA-256 (or stronger) checksums for any binary artifacts and include verification instructions.

Chain-of-custody & forensic handling requirements:
- Collection checklist: Each artifact must include a short collection report signed/initialed by the collector, with UTC timestamps, tool/version used, and rationale.
- Transport: Artifacts must be delivered via mutually agreed secure channel (SFTP with client certs, signed transfer link, or encrypted archive with pre-shared key exchange) and a record of transfer success.
- Retention: Vendor retains a copy of delivered artifacts for no longer than 90 days post-delivery unless otherwise agreed.

Subprocessor obligations and onboarding:
- Subprocessor flow-down: Vendor must require subprocessors to adhere to the same segregation and evidence SLAs when subprocessors process Customer Data.
- Subprocessor disclosures: On execution and annually, vendor will provide a list of subprocessors with a summary of what processing they perform and which geographic regions they operate in.
- Rapid substitution: In case a subprocessor cannot meet evidence requirements, vendor must propose an alternative or commit to absorbing the evidence obligation directly.

Encryption and key management expectations:
- BYOK/HSM: For customers requesting BYOK, vendor should support either HSM-backed key wrapping or integration with customer KMS in a supported region.
- Key separation: Encryption key contexts should be per-customer where practical. Where shared keys are used, vendor must disclose and produce key usage logs on evidence requests (not raw keys).
- Key rotation: Vendor will document rotation frequency and provide rotation events as part of artifact sets if relevant to the request.

Data deletion, return, and proof-of-wipe:
- Return: After termination, vendor shall return Customer Data in an agreed format within 30 days unless a different timeframe is negotiated for large-scale exports.
- Deletion: Vendor will securely delete residual copies and provide Proof-of-Deletion (cryptographic erasure logs, sanitized index lists, or storage provider deletion receipts).
- On-prem nuance: For on-prem/private deployments where vendor personnel performs tape destruction, proof should include signed disposal receipts and photographs where permitted by customer policy.

Redaction, minimal disclosure, and privacy-preserving evidence:
- Minimize PII: Where possible, vendor should redact unrelated customer or third-party PII before artifact delivery while preserving forensic value. Redaction methods and tooling must be documented.
- Separate export of PII: If full PII export is required for an investigation, the vendor will request explicit written authorization from the customer and document the legal basis.

Audit, on-site inspection, and third-party attestation:
- Remote evidence access: Preferred mechanism; vendor provides secured remote sessions to observe artifacts in situ under a documented process.
- Onsite inspections: Allowed with reasonable notice (typical: 30 days) and under mutual NDAs; vendor may charge cost recovery for travel and facility access but should not unreasonably withhold.
- Certifications: Vendor will maintain, at minimum, SOC 2 Type II and provide an annual scope map indicating which services are covered. Additional certifications (ISO 27001, FedRAMP, etc.) should be listed where applicable.

Forensics support and engagement model:
- Escalation path: Provide primary security contact, secondary contact, and legal contact with 24/7 contactability for confirmed incidents.
- Forensics retainer: Vendor to describe whether a dedicated forensics retainer is required for deep-dive engagements and cost model.

Change control and notification obligations:
- Changes to isolation architecture, subprocessors, or key management approach must be notified 60 days in advance for customers with contractual protections; for critical security fixes, vendor must notify no later than 30 days post-change and provide impact assessment.

Negotiation notes and fallback positions (internal):
- Customers will often ask for per-customer HSM keys; vendor can offer per-tenant encryption context as compromise unless customer pays for BYOK.
- Artifact timelines can be extended for physical/on-prem cases; include explicit carve-outs.
- If vendor cannot provide raw memory images, offer parsed extracts plus a sealed-forensics review by mutually agreed third-party.

Annex A: Evidence Request form (example)
- Requestor: [CUSTOMER_NAME], authorized contact and email
- Scope: [Specify systems, time windows, data classes]
- Artifacts requested: [logs, snapshots, configs, KV-dumps, cache-eviction records]
- Purpose: [e.g. incident response, regulatory inquiry, litigation hold]
- Sensitive handling required: [yes/no]
- Delivery preference: [secure link / SFTP / on-site]
- Signed authorization: [Yes/No] - attach if required

Annex B: Example timeline (typical hosted service)
- Day 0: Evidence Request submitted.
- Day 1: Acknowledgement.
- Day 3: Containment assessment + artifact list.
- Day 10: Delivery of preserved artifacts.
- Day 15: Proof-of-Deletion (if applicable).

Open items and TODOs for legal negotiation:
- Decide whether Proof-of-Deletion can be an affidavit vs. technical artifact for specific storage backends.
- Confirm chargeback policy for on-site audits and whether travel costs are billable.
- Define whether vendor will accept a third-party neutral forensic verifier and process for appointment.
- Map which parts of this exhibit are mandatory vs. optional for different product tiers (hosted API vs Dedicated vs Private).

Internal references and cross-links:
- Confluence: SEC-Data-Isolation-Playbook (internal runbook)
- JIRA: SEC-2147 (evidence SLA exceptions)
- Legal precedent: clause bank entry LP-011 (evidence handling templates)

Usage guidance for contracting teams:
- Start with this template as an annex to the DPA for customers with elevated data isolation needs.
- For enterprise customers, consider adding explicit BYOK options and faster evidence timelines for an additional fee.
- For Private/on-prem customers, convert SLAs into operational runbooks and attach implementation notes specific to the deployment.

Versioning and authorship:
- Drafted by: Asha Menon (security-and-compliance)
- Contributors: Ethan Park, Marisol Rivera, Trevor Shaw, Priya Kapoor
- Version: v0.9-draft (for internal review)

End of playbook (template).

Negotiation-ready snippet (short clause to insert into DPA):
"Vendor shall maintain logical and administrative segregation of Customer Data in accordance with the Vendor Data Isolation & Evidence Delivery Playbook attached as Exhibit X. Upon receipt of a written Evidence Request, Vendor shall acknowledge the request within 24 hours and provide preserved artifacts in accordance with the timelines in Exhibit X, subject to exceptions for on-prem and physical media. Vendor shall cause its subprocessors to comply with the material obligations in Exhibit X and shall remain responsible for evidence delivery as if the Vendor performed the processing itself."
"Note: [insert customer-specific BYOK, audit frequency, and onsite inspection carve-outs as negotiated]."
